You get a top RB in whoever is left over from Lacy, Peterson, Lynch, Bell, and Charles and then the swing comes around sooner so you can grab a top WR in round 2. I've seen Nelson and Dez fall to me, but more often I'm getting a guy like Cobb or Green there and I love it.

In our league it's better to be on the ends of the snake, the middle misses those crucial first picks and then the next 8-15 top tier go to the last picks. By the 3rd round you don't have an elite Top 5, have a top tier and a top 20, and you're picking ~#40. The end of the snake might not have the #5-#7 pick, but they'll still have 2 great players by the middle's second pick.

Since the LT era ended, I've always liked the 3-6 spots. You get a good pick, and if #3-4, you can easily manage those snake picks where you know you can wait on your need, and snake theirs, if they have your need covered. (If that makes sense - lol)

I plan to attend Temple University soon, which is an English speaking university in Japan. I want to major in Computer Science. My japanese is okay, but obviously I plan to improve my speaking skills. I'm a foreigner, from America, and I'm wondering if me being a foreigner affects me getting a job positively, negatively, or no effect at all. How does it compare working in the computer/gaming industry in Japan and America? Also, is there a major difference in salaries or are they just slight? Thanks!
Is it easier or harder to get a job with computers/games in Japan than America?

I work at a software company in Tokyo, like you I am an American. I did my masters degree at the University of Hiroshima. It was an absolutely fantastic experience and definitely life changing, I recommend it 100% with no reservations. In terms of getting a job back home it's essentially like hitting a solid triple while most folks are lucky to get to first base. The weight that the experience carries on your resume can be quite strong with some people. Others won't give a damn. If you also pick up the language its even more of a win, study hard, stay focused on your goals. I saw plenty of people lose sight of their goals and turn their experience into an extra long vacation, can't particularly recommend that route, but to each their own I suppose.

On a personal level, you'll probably feel a bit like Goku, training with the extra heavy suit on. The amount of perception altering experiences you will have will be incredible. You will feel, think, and process a lot of things very differently from your friends who did not travel abroad for school - this will probably manifest itself as reverse culture shock when you get back home. Your friends will still be sitting at the same bar they did before, doing the same things, telling the same jokes. You will probably find yourself baffled at how much they are missing out on.

Salaries in Japan are notably lower. In fact, its a general rule of thumb that for IT, Japan is lowest of the first world countries, Europe is between Japan and the States, and California / Boston are the most expensive - and I'm not even sure it makes mathematical sense the salaries can be as high as they are in those regions.

At the same time, not necessarily the raw pay-rate, but the quality of life you can enjoy for what you earn is worth a good look. I won't say one is better than the other, I live in Japan now, but Japan is not better than the US. Additionally, the US is not better than Japan, they're different. Right now, with what I personally want to do and experience and the lifestyle I want to live, Japan is a good match for me. It probably won't be forever, but now its a better fit. Try to be mindful of these differences so you can make your own educated decision on whether or not you want to continue living here.

Some of the major differences, I think, are the lack of unexpected bills. In the US two very common and very annoying unexpected bills include medical bills and car repair, both of which I had the unpleasant situation of experiencing in the States. Living in Tokyo, I don't have a car, and the health insurance here is second to none, that would have saved me a boat load.

If you have any other questions you would like me to follow up on, let me know.

Thank you so much! If you don't mind me asking, what made you interested to work and complete your masters degree in Japan? Also, how is the work environment for you being a foreigner with majority of your colleagues being native to Japan I suppose?

Work environment is great. Though experiences may vary, like any job, depends on if you like what you do, what your personal goals are etc. I'd say there is no higher or lower chance of being satisfied with your career than if it were in a different country. A lot depends on company culture, do you get along with colleagues, etc. So you could have equally difficult/easy time at two different companies in Texas, or anywhere else.

I became interested in Japan when my friend and I were enormously dorky, and he went to Japan as an exchange student and landed one of the most banging hot girlfriends he, I or any of our friends had ever seen. After that I started studying the language. After that, I felt if I didn't become fluent, I'd have wasted those years studying. Best way to get fluent, live there. Did that. Met a girl, married, grad school, kids, more grad school... Now I've got a kid that I'd like to support a nice life for, and I'd like to have a few toys myself...so bada bing bada boom I get a job.

I also work for a software company in Tokyo. What DrJokimoto said is spot on. Salaries are not great here and living spaces are very small. As long as these realities don't bother you, you will have a great time!
